body:
What makes a microorganism harmful?

A microorganism capable of causing disease is called a pathogen. Pathogens may enter a person's body, multiply or interfere with normal body functions, and cause illness.

Not every microorganism is pathogenic. Many microbes normally present in soil, food or the human body are harmless or beneficial.

Communicable diseases

A communicable disease is an infectious disease that can spread from one host to another, directly or indirectly.

Pathogens may spread through air, contaminated food or water, direct physical contact, contaminated objects or carriers such as certain insects.

Major human diseases caused by microorganisms

DiseaseCausing agentMain transmission
TuberculosisBacteriumAirborne transmission
CholeraBacteriumContaminated food or water
Typhoid feverBacteriumContaminated food or water
Common coldVirusesRespiratory transmission
InfluenzaVirusRespiratory transmission
MeaslesVirusAirborne transmission
ChickenpoxVirusAirborne transmission or contact
PolioVirusPrimarily faecal-oral transmission
Hepatitis AVirusContaminated food or water
MalariaProtozoanInfected female Anopheles mosquito
DengueVirusInfected Aedes mosquito
Amoebic dysenteryProtozoanContaminated food or water

The disease and its causative organism must be distinguished from the method by which it spreads. For example, malaria is caused by a protozoan, but a mosquito transmits the parasite.

Airborne and respiratory transmission

When an infected person coughs, sneezes, speaks or breathes, infectious particles may enter the surrounding air. Other people may inhale these particles and become infected.

Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria, while influenza and the common cold are caused by viruses. Therefore, similar transmission routes do not necessarily indicate the same type of pathogen.

Foodborne and waterborne transmission

Food and drinking water may become contaminated with disease-causing microorganisms, particularly where sanitation and safe water facilities are inadequate.

Cholera and typhoid are bacterial diseases commonly associated with contaminated food or water. Hepatitis A and polio are viral diseases that can also spread through the faecal-oral route.

Faecal-oral transmission occurs when pathogens from infected faecal matter enter another person's mouth, often through contaminated hands, food or water.

Carriers and vectors

Some insects help pathogens move from one place or host to another.

Housefly

A housefly may land on garbage or animal excreta and collect pathogens on its body. When it subsequently lands on uncovered food, it can mechanically transfer those pathogens to the food.

Mosquitoes

Certain mosquitoes transmit pathogens when they bite an infected host and later bite another susceptible host.

  • Female Anopheles mosquito: Transmits the Plasmodium parasite that causes malaria.
  • Female Aedes mosquito: Transmits dengue virus.

In these examples, the mosquito is the vector, while the protozoan or virus is the actual disease-causing agent.

Prevention of communicable diseases

Different transmission routes require appropriate preventive measures.

  • Respiratory infections: Follow respiratory hygiene, cover coughs and sneezes, improve ventilation and follow recommended vaccination measures.
  • Foodborne and waterborne infections: Use safe drinking water, maintain sanitation, wash hands and protect food from contamination.
  • Mosquito-borne infections: Prevent water from stagnating in containers, use suitable mosquito protection and reduce mosquito breeding places.
  • Contact-related infections: Maintain personal hygiene and avoid contact with infectious materials.

Vaccination provides protection against several specific infections, but it does not replace sanitation, safe water or vector control.

Dysentery describes an illness rather than a single microorganism. Amoebic dysentery is caused by a protozoan, but some other forms of dysentery are caused by bacteria.

Prelims focus

  • Cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis are bacterial diseases.
  • Polio, measles, chickenpox and dengue are viral diseases.
  • Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium.
  • Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria.
  • Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue virus.
  • Trap: Dengue and malaria are both mosquito-borne, but their pathogens belong to different groups.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, section Harmful Microorganisms and Table 2.1, pp. 22–24, 2018–19; NCERT, Health and Physical Education: A Teachers' Guide for Class 6, Unit 7, pp. 118–121; World Health Organization, Poliomyelitis, Overview and Transmission, accessed 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Pathogens reach people through respiratory particles, contaminated food, water or hands, housefly transfer, and mosquitoes carrying malaria or dengue pathogens.
pictures.caption: Pathogens may reach humans through respiratory particles, contaminated food or insect vectors.

title: Harmful Microorganisms: Human Diseases and Modes of Transmission

body:
Why microorganisms matter in agriculture and animal health

Some microorganisms infect crops and domestic animals. These infections may reduce crop yield, damage plant tissues, affect animal health and cause economic losses.

The important distinction is between the organism causing the disease, the plant or animal affected, and the method of transmission.

Diseases of crop plants

Bacteria, fungi and viruses can all cause plant diseases.

Plant diseaseCauseImportant feature
Citrus cankerBacteriaInfects citrus plants; may spread through air-driven rain and infected plant material
Rust of wheatFungiFungal disease; spores may spread through air and contaminated material
Yellow vein mosaic of bhindiVirusViral disease spread by insect vectors

Citrus canker

Citrus canker is a bacterial disease affecting citrus plants. It can produce characteristic lesions on affected plant parts. The infection may spread through contaminated planting material and wind-driven rain.

Rust of wheat

Wheat rust is caused by fungi. The disease may produce rust-coloured pustules on infected plant parts. Fungal spores can spread between plants, especially through air.

Yellow vein mosaic of bhindi

Yellow vein mosaic of bhindi, also called okra, is a viral disease. It causes noticeable yellowing of leaf veins and can spread through insect vectors.

The insect transmits the virus; the insect itself is not the virus.

Microbial diseases of animals

Anthrax

Anthrax is a dangerous bacterial disease caused by Bacillus anthracis. It can affect cattle and other animals and can also infect human beings.

Thus, anthrax is not exclusively an animal disease, even though it is particularly important in livestock health.

Foot-and-mouth disease

Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cattle and certain other cloven-hoofed animals.

It is caused by a virus, not by a bacterium or fungus. It must also not be confused with hand, foot and mouth disease, a different viral illness that mainly affects young children.

General prevention and control

The spread of microbial diseases in plants and animals can be reduced through suitable preventive practices.

  • Using healthy seeds and disease-free planting material reduces the introduction of crop pathogens.
  • Controlling insects that transmit plant viruses can reduce the spread of vector-borne crop diseases.
  • Removing or appropriately managing infected plant material may reduce further transmission.
  • Good hygiene, veterinary care and recommended vaccination help control certain animal diseases.

The effective method depends on whether the disease is bacterial, fungal or viral and on the way the pathogen spreads.

Prelims focus

  • Citrus canker is caused by bacteria.
  • Rust of wheat is caused by fungi.
  • Yellow vein mosaic of bhindi is caused by a virus.
  • Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis.
  • Foot-and-mouth disease of cattle is viral.
  • Trap: A disease transmitted by insects is not necessarily caused by insects.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections Disease-Causing Microorganisms in Animals and Disease-Causing Microorganisms in Plants, Table 2.2, pp. 24–25, 2018–19; GCERT, Science, Std. 8, Ch. 2, pp. 24–25.]

pictures.alt: An insect carries a virus from infected bhindi with yellow leaf veins to healthy bhindi; the virus causes disease and the insect transmits it.
pictures.caption: Insect vectors can transfer plant viruses between infected and healthy crops.

title: Microbial Diseases of Plants and Animals

body:
What is immunity?

Human beings are exposed to many microorganisms through their surroundings. The body has natural defence mechanisms that help prevent infection and fight microorganisms that enter it.

Immunity is the body's ability to defend itself against particular infections or harmful substances.

The immune system includes different kinds of cells and protective substances. White blood cells play important roles in identifying and responding to infectious agents.

How the immune system recognises pathogens

When a disease-causing microorganism enters the body, the immune system may recognise particular substances associated with it.

A substance that can be recognised by the immune system and trigger a specific immune response is called an antigen.

The body can respond by producing antibodies, which are proteins that bind to particular antigens.

Antibodies can help block pathogens or make them easier for other immune cells to destroy. Different antibodies recognise different antigens.

Immune memory

When the immune system first encounters a particular pathogen, developing a strong response may take time.

After the response, specialised immune cells may remain capable of recognising the same pathogen or its antigens. This is called immune memory.

If the same pathogen enters the body again, immune memory may allow a faster and more effective response.

However, the strength and duration of protection vary between infections and individuals. Having an infection once does not guarantee permanent immunity against every future infection.

What is a vaccine?

A vaccine is a biological preparation designed to stimulate the immune system to develop protection against a particular disease.

Vaccines expose the immune system to a suitable antigen or instructions for producing an antigen without requiring the person to experience the disease itself.

Different vaccines may contain weakened microorganisms, inactivated microorganisms or selected components of a pathogen. The central purpose is to train the immune system to recognise the disease-causing agent.

How vaccination produces protection

  1. A vaccine introduces an appropriate antigen or causes the body to produce it.
  2. The immune system recognises the antigen and begins responding.
  3. Specific antibodies and immune memory may develop.
  4. If the actual pathogen is encountered later, the immune system can respond more effectively.

Vaccination reduces the risk of particular infections or their serious consequences. It is primarily a preventive measure, not a medicine used to directly kill pathogens in an existing infection.

Vaccination and the duration of protection

Different vaccines provide protection for different lengths of time. Some produce long-lasting immunity, while others require additional doses.

A booster dose is an additional vaccine dose given when recommended to strengthen or maintain protection.

No vaccine guarantees 100% protection for every individual. Nevertheless, vaccination can substantially reduce the likelihood of disease and, for many vaccines, the risk of severe illness.

Community protection

When a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune to a transmissible disease, the pathogen may have fewer opportunities to spread.

This reduction in transmission can indirectly protect some people who are not immune. The effect is commonly called herd immunity or community protection.

Its effectiveness depends on the disease, how it spreads and how well immunity prevents transmission. It is not a substitute for recommended individual vaccination.

Antigen: A substance recognised by the immune system.
Antibody: A protective protein that binds to a particular antigen.
Vaccine: A preparation used to stimulate protective immunity.
Vaccination: Administration of a vaccine.

Prelims focus

  • White blood cells are important components of the immune system.
  • Antigens stimulate specific immune responses.
  • Antibodies recognise and bind to particular antigens.
  • Immune memory helps the body respond more rapidly to a previously encountered pathogen.
  • Vaccination is primarily preventive.
  • Trap: Vaccination reduces disease risk but does not guarantee permanent or complete protection.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, section Vaccine, p. 21, 2018–19; World Health Organization, How Do Vaccines Work, sections The Body's Natural Response, How Vaccines Help and Herd Immunity, accessed 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, Vaccine Efficacy, Effectiveness and Protection, sections Boosters and Vaccine Protection and Infection, accessed 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Vaccination leads to antigen recognition, antibodies and immune memory, which can improve the response to the same pathogen later; protection varies.
pictures.caption: Vaccination prepares the immune system to respond more effectively to a later infection.

title: Immunity and Vaccines: How the Body Develops Protection

body:
Why vaccination programmes are organised

Vaccination protects individuals against specific infectious diseases. When vaccination reaches large numbers of people, it can also help prevent outbreaks and reduce the burden of disease.

Governments organise immunization programmes to make recommended vaccines accessible to eligible groups, particularly children.

Universal Immunization Programme

India introduced the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1978. In 1985, it was expanded and renamed the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

The UIP provides routine immunization services through India's public health system. It includes vaccines against important childhood diseases and vaccination services for eligible pregnant women.

Examples of vaccine-preventable diseases covered through routine immunization include polio, measles, tuberculosis and several other infections.

The programme applies across India, including Gujarat. Vaccination services are delivered through the public health system, including government health facilities and organised immunization sessions.

Pulse Polio Immunization Programme

Poliomyelitis, commonly called polio, is caused by a virus. It can damage the nervous system and may cause paralysis.

India began nationwide Pulse Polio immunization campaigns in 1995 to strengthen efforts against polio.

These campaigns are particularly associated with the administration of oral polio vaccine drops to all children under 5 years of age, regardless of previous polio vaccination.

The campaigns complement routine immunization by helping reach children who might otherwise miss vaccination.

India's polio milestone

India's last reported case of wild poliovirus infection occurred on 13 January 2011.

On 27 March 2014, the World Health Organization's South-East Asia Region, which includes India, was certified free of wild poliovirus.

This achievement required vaccination, surveillance and public health efforts.

India's certification as polio-free in 2014 does not mean that polio was eradicated from the entire world. National or regional elimination and global eradication are different achievements.

Smallpox and the development of vaccination

Edward Jenner demonstrated the protective effect of cowpox inoculation against smallpox in 1796. He published his findings in 1798. His work became a major foundation of modern vaccination.

Smallpox was caused by the variola virus. A global vaccination and disease-control campaign eventually eliminated naturally occurring smallpox.

The World Health Assembly officially declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

Smallpox remains the first human infectious disease to have been eradicated worldwide.

Key historical milestones

These dates describe established historical milestones. Vaccination schedules, eligibility details and campaign arrangements may change over time. The programme descriptions here are considered at the 3 November 2026 content cutoff and are not intended to reproduce a current vaccination schedule.

Prelims focus

  • 1978: Expanded Programme on Immunization introduced in India.
  • 1985: Universal Immunization Programme established.
  • 1995: Nationwide Pulse Polio campaigns began.
  • 13 January 2011: India's last reported wild polio case.
  • 27 March 2014: WHO South-East Asia Region certified polio-free.
  • 1980: WHO declared global eradication of smallpox.
  • Trap: Jenner demonstrated the first successful smallpox vaccination in 1796; his findings were published in 1798.

[National Health Mission, Immunization, Background Note, accessed 3 November 2026; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Pulse Polio Programme in India, pp. 1–2, historical programme milestones; World Health Organization, India: A Push to Vaccinate Every Child, Everywhere, Ended Polio in India, 7 April 2021; World Health Organization, History of Smallpox Vaccination, section on Edward Jenner, and Smallpox, Overview, accessed 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Childhood vaccination is an important public health service in India, including Gujarat.
